A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adjoint-based PDE-discovery work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching experiments and derivations moved into different appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original numerical PDE-discovery experiments, including coefficient errors and execution times for heat, Burgers’, Kuramoto–Sivashinsky, random-walk, and reaction-diffusion examples.

after.justification: V2 retains original numerical experiments and adds temporal-sparsity, gradient-averaging, thresholding, and travelling-wave results.

M1.justification: Section 2 replaces the full-trajectory objective and solves with observation-interval losses and solves initialized from each observation. V2 adds squared-L2 coefficient regularization, thresholding during and after training, and Algorithm 2’s averaged-gradient updates. These change the reported optimization procedure.

E1.justification: V2 adds travelling-wave data, f(x,t) = sin(x−t), to investigate discovery when multiple PDEs fit the observations (Section 6 and Appendix B.5). All five original equation/process families remain; temporal subsampling of the retained heat data is a protocol change.

E2.justification: The noise comparison expands from Adjoint versus PDE-FIND in v1 Figure 13 to averaged Adjoint, unaveraged Adjoint, and PDE-FIND in v2 Figure 3. PDE-FIND/STRidge remains the external baseline; no additional external comparison method is evaluated.

E3.justification: The retained noise experiments change from unfiltered observations to SVD denoising with a cutoff of O(10^-4). New protocols thin heat observations by factors of 1–16 while retaining 1000 solver steps. The travelling-wave experiment uses six derivative candidates and 100 internal solver steps per observation interval.

E4.justification: Beyond v1’s grid/sample-size and noise studies, v2 adds temporal-sparsity sensitivity (Figure 2/Table 1), averaging versus no averaging under noise (Figure 3), active-thresholding controls for Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (Figure 7), and a non-uniqueness case study (Section 6/Appendix B.5).

E5.justification: V1 does not specify repeated timing runs or uncertainty estimation. V2 Section 3 reports execution times averaged over ten independent runs and standard-deviation error bars. This establishes newly reported statistical practice, not an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: New Table 1 reports recovery of f_t−f_xx=0 at all five temporal sampling fractions, after rounding, while PDE-FIND develops spurious terms under thinning. The wave example reports advection coefficients 0.996 for Adjoint and 0.9897 for PDE-FIND. Noise results are replaced under revised preprocessing, and thresholding results are added. V1 Table 1’s Fokker–Planck coefficients remain unchanged in v2 Table 2.

T1.justification: Section 2 and the illustrative appendices substantially revise the objective, gradient, and adjoint derivations for discrete observation losses and regularization, removing the continuous error-forcing term. V2 also adds an explicit family of non-unique PDEs. Its worked first-derivative updates in Appendix C introduce signs inconsistent with the stated gradient-descent rule, whereas v1’s corresponding updates have the consistent signs.

C1.justification: The abstract removes v1’s explicit claim that noisy-data accuracy becomes comparable to PDE-FIND, replacing it with a statement that smooth and noisy data are compared. The central PDE-discovery contribution, noise-free accuracy claim in the conclusion, and large-data efficiency claim remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive discussion of non-uniqueness and regularization, distinguishes temporal refinement from spatial-resolution constraints, and identifies failure when the underlying PDE lacks a stable numerical solver. Its noise interpretation now emphasizes averaging’s accuracy/cost tradeoff, replacing v1’s emphasis on both methods failing at high noise.

D1.justification: V2 supplies explicit defaults for thresholding (10^-3 after 100 epochs), convergence tolerance (10^-9), and regularization (10^-12), plus SVD filtering and internal solver-step details. Much existing documentation of data generation, candidate libraries, discretizations, and CPU hardware is retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds Flath et al. (2011) on uncertainty quantification and removes Li et al. (2020)’s Fourier-neural-operator citation. The introduction more explicitly distinguishes discovering PDE form from conventional adjoint optimization with known governing equations. The principal related-work discussion remains.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: four original benchmark subsections move to Appendix B, the derivations move from Appendix A to C, and dedicated main-text sections foreground temporal sparsity, noise, and ill-posedness. The method description and algorithm presentation are extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Original heat figures are merged, noise and thresholding displays are expanded, and many benchmark figures relocate to Appendix B. V2 adds a temporal-sparsity table and plots, algorithm flowcharts, and travelling-wave plots.

improvement.justification: V2 provides useful additional robustness evidence, explicit optimization controls, timing uncertainty, and clearer applicability limits. These improve evaluation and reproducibility. The net gain is tempered by newly inconsistent signs in Appendix C’s worked updates and an insufficiently supported attribution of minimum-term recovery to L2 regularization despite also using thresholding.
